title: Jeremiah 1:11–19
context: The LORD’s word comes again to Jeremiah, still in the prophet’s first-person report, now in two visions. The LORD asks what he sees, and Jeremiah says he sees a branch of an almond tree. The LORD answers that he has seen well, “for I watch over my word to perform it.” In Hebrew the word for the almond and the word for watching are close in sound, and many readers take the vision as a wordplay that English cannot fully carry; that observation may be offered in plain words and should stay hedged, not pressed as a reconstruction of the text. A second time the LORD asks what he sees, and Jeremiah sees a boiling cauldron tipping away from the north. The LORD says that out of the north evil will break out on all the inhabitants of the land, and that he will call the families of the kingdoms of the north to set their thrones at the gates of Jerusalem, because the people have forsaken him and burned incense to other gods. Jeremiah is told to put his belt on, arise, and say all that he is commanded, and not to be dismayed. The LORD has made him a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against kings, princes, priests, and people; they will fight him, but they will not prevail, for the LORD is with him to rescue him. The foe from the north is not named in this unit; later chapters, with 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52, will tell of a coming from that direction, and those accounts may be named without being read back as if this vision had already supplied the name. For how God relates to hostile agents, the existing box at Judges 9:23 may be consulted; a new contrast is not needed here.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying, “Jeremiah, what do you see?” I said, “I see a branch of an almond tree.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Moreover the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying, “Jeremiah, what do you see?” And he said, “I see a branch of an almond tree.” The first vision is simple: a question, and a seen branch. The almond is an early tree in its season, which some readers connect with the swiftness of the word; that link should stay light until the next verse, where the LORD interprets what was seen.

Arminian readers take the question and the answer as a real exchange. Jeremiah sees what he is shown and names it; the meaning will be given, not guessed as a private symbol system.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive a genuine vision and a plain report: a branch of an almond tree. The LORD is teaching his prophet to see, and then to hear the word that goes with the sight.

Shared ground: the vision is of an almond branch, reported in dialogue. There is no party contrast over what Jeremiah saw.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “You have seen well; for I watch over my word to perform it.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD said, “You have seen well; for I watch over my word to perform it.” The sight is confirmed, and the meaning is the LORD’s watchfulness over his own word, to perform it. In Hebrew the name of the almond and the verb for watching are close, so the vision may turn on a wordplay that the English line cannot fully reproduce. That is a common observation offered in plain words; it is not a claim about another wording of the verse, and it should not be pressed beyond what this English text already says: the LORD watches over his word to perform it.

Arminian readers hear a promise that the word given to Jeremiah will be performed, a watchfulness that stands behind the prophet’s speech and does not cancel the need for Judah to hear it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the line as the LORD’s own pledge: he watches over his word to perform it. The possible Hebrew wordplay, if mentioned, only underlines that pledge; it does not become a separate doctrine or a textual theory.

Shared ground: God watches over his word and will perform it. The wordplay, if it is present, is a help to readers, not a fork between the traditions.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me the second time, saying, “What do you see?” I said, “I see a boiling cauldron; and it is tipping away from the north.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word came “the second time,” saying, “What do you see?” Jeremiah said, “I see a boiling cauldron; and it is tipping away from the north.” The second sight is a pot on the boil, tilted from the north. The exact picture—how the pot sits, and how its contents would pour—should be described modestly and not turned into a map the verse does not draw.

Arminian readers take the second vision as another real showing, to be interpreted by the word that follows, not as an allegory to be filled in from later history before the LORD has spoken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from what is seen: a boiling cauldron tipping away from the north. The meaning will be given in the next lines, and the later story of invasion need not be imported faster than the text allows.

Both traditions wait for the LORD’s explanation. There is no party contrast over the shape of the pot.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “Out of the north, evil will break out on all the inhabitants of the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD said, “Out of the north, evil will break out on all the inhabitants of the land.” The boiling pot is read as calamity coming from the north upon the whole land. The evil is the disaster announced, not a claim that God is the author of wickedness in the hearts of the invaders. The foe is not named here. Later narrative may be compared, without treating this line as already having said Babylon. How God relates to hostile agents is already treated in the existing box at Judges 9:23; that discussion need not be restated, and no new contrast is required.

Arminian readers hear a real warning of coming disaster from the north, a word the people are meant to take to heart, not a hidden schedule that leaves no room for the judgments and the calls that follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the announcement as the LORD’s own word: evil will break out from the north on all the inhabitants of the land. They may hear his sovereignty in the coming of that disaster, while still pointing to the existing box at Judges 9:23.

Shared ground: a calamity from the north is announced against the land. The verse does not name the enemy, and it is not a new contrast over providence.

verses.text: For behold, I will call all the families of the kingdoms of the north,” says the LORD. “They will come, and they will each set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all its walls all around, and against all the cities of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For behold, I will call all the families of the kingdoms of the north,” says the LORD. “They will come, and they will each set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all its walls all around, and against all the cities of Judah.” The LORD himself calls these families. They will sit as if in judgment at the gates, and the whole land is in view, not only the capital.

Arminian readers take the calling of the northern kingdoms as the LORD’s real act in history, a judgment he announces, while the coming kings remain responsible for what they do at the gates.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same “I will call” as the LORD’s sovereign summons of the northern families, by which he brings them against Jerusalem and Judah, without denying their willing part in the siege this picture implies.

Shared ground: the threat is from the north, at the gates and walls, and it is the LORD who says he will call them. The verse still does not name the later empire.

verses.text: I will utter my judgments against them concerning all their wickedness, in that they have forsaken me, and have burned incense to other gods, and worshiped the works of their own hands.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will utter my judgments against them concerning all their wickedness, in that they have forsaken me, and have burned incense to other gods, and worshiped the works of their own hands.” The coming disaster is not unexplained. The LORD will utter judgments because of wickedness: they have forsaken him, burned incense to other gods, and worshiped what their hands have made.

Arminian readers take the three charges as real guilt, a forsaking the people could have refused. The judgment is answered to that wickedness, not a fate announced without cause.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also ground the judgments in the people’s wickedness: forsaking the LORD, incense to other gods, and worship of handmade works. The LORD utters what is just, and the guilt named here is their own.

Both traditions share the indictment. There is no party contrast over the reasons given in this verse.

verses.text: “You therefore put your belt on your waist, arise, and say to them all that I command you. Don’t be dismayed at them, lest I dismay you before them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You therefore put your belt on your waist, arise, and say to them all that I command you.” Then, “Don’t be dismayed at them, lest I dismay you before them.” Jeremiah is to get ready, stand up, and speak the whole command. Fear of the audience is itself a danger: if he is dismayed at them, the LORD warns that he may dismay Jeremiah before them.

Arminian readers hear a charge that calls for courage in speech, a real warning to a prophet who might shrink, not a promise that dismay is impossible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same command as the LORD’s hold on his prophet: he must speak all that he is commanded, and the warning against dismay is as serious as the sending.

Shared ground: the prophet is to arise and speak, and he is not to be dismayed at those who hear. The verse looks forward to conflict, not to ease.

verses.text: For behold, I have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land—against the kings of Judah, against its princes, against its priests, and against the people of the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For behold, I have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land—against the kings of Judah, against its princes, against its priests, and against the people of the land.” The “today” matches the commission. Jeremiah is made to stand, like a city and like metal walls, against every rank of the land, including priests and kings, not only against a foreign foe.

Arminian readers take the images as the LORD’s pledge to make his prophet able to stand, a strengthening given for a ministry that will meet real opposition from his own people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same making as the LORD’s work: he has made Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls. The strength is given, not self-made, and it is given against the whole land.

Shared ground: the prophet’s standing is the LORD’s doing, and the opposition named includes Judah’s own leaders and people.

verses.text: They will fight against you, but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says the LORD, “to rescue you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will fight against you, but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says the LORD, “to rescue you.” Opposition is certain, and so is the promise already heard in 1:8. They will fight and will not prevail; the LORD is with him to rescue him. The pledge does not mean that Jeremiah will be spared struggle, only that he will not be overcome.

Arminian readers take both halves as real: a fight that will come, and a rescue they can trust, spoken to a prophet who must still stand and speak.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hold the fight and the promise together. The LORD’s “I am with you” and “to rescue you” are the ground of the word that the opponents will not prevail.

Both traditions share the close of the call. The presence and rescue are the LORD’s, and they do not cancel the fight announced in the same breath.
